# Skill: understand

# /understand

Analyze the current codebase and produce a `knowledge-graph.json` file in the project's data directory (`.ua/`, or the legacy `.understand-anything/` when it already exists). This file powers the interactive dashboard for exploring the project's architecture.

## Options

- `$ARGUMENTS` may contain:
  - `--full` — Force a full rebuild, ignoring any existing graph
  - `--auto-update` — Enable automatic graph updates on commit (writes `autoUpdate: true` to `$UA_DIR/config.json`)
  - `--no-auto-update` — Disable automatic graph updates (writes `autoUpdate: false` to `$UA_DIR/config.json`)
  - `--review` — Run full LLM graph-reviewer instead of inline deterministic validation
  - `--language <lang>` — Generate all textual content (summaries, descriptions, tags, titles, languageNotes, languageLesson) in the specified language. Accepts ISO 639-1 codes (`zh`, `ja`, `ko`, `en`, `es`, `fr`, `de`, etc.) or friendly names (`chinese`, `japanese`, `korean`, `english`, `spanish`, etc.). Locale variants supported: `zh-TW`, `zh-HK`, etc. Defaults to `en` (English). Stores preference in `$UA_DIR/config.json` for consistency across incremental updates.
  - `--exclude <patterns>` — Comma-separated glob patterns for additional files/directories to exclude from analysis (e.g., `--exclude "tests/*,docs/*"`). These patterns take highest priority over built-in defaults and `.understandignore` rules. Supports gitignore syntax including `!` negation.
  - A directory path (e.g. `/path/to/repo` or `../other-project`) — Analyze the given directory instead of the current working directory

---

## Progress Reporting

Throughout execution, report progress to the user at each phase transition and during batch processing. This keeps users informed on large codebases where analysis can take a long time.

- **Phase transitions:** At the start of each phase, print a status line:
  > `[Phase N/7] <phase name>...`
  >
  > Example: `[Phase 2/7] Analyzing files (12 batches)...`

- **Batch progress:** During Phase 2, report each batch with its index and total:
  > `Analyzing batch X/N (files: foo.ts, bar.ts, ...)` (list up to 3 filenames, then `...` if more)

- **Phase completion:** When a phase finishes, briefly confirm:
  > `Phase N complete. <one-line summary of result>`
  >
  > Example: `Phase 1 complete. Found 247 files across 3 languages.`

Detect a worktree by comparing `git rev-parse --git-dir` against `git rev-parse --git-common-dir`; in a normal checkout or submodule they resolve to the same path, in a worktree they differ and the parent of `--git-common-dir` is the main repo root.

     ```bash
     COMMON_DIR=$(git -C "$PROJECT_ROOT" rev-parse --git-common-dir 2>/dev/null)
     GIT_DIR=$(git -C "$PROJECT_ROOT" rev-parse --git-dir 2>/dev/null)
     if [ -n "$COMMON_DIR" ] && [ -n "$GIT_DIR" ]; then

       GIT_ABS=$(cd "$PROJECT_ROOT" && cd "$GIT_DIR" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P)
       if [ -n "$COMMON_ABS" ] && [ "$COMMON_ABS" != "$GIT_ABS" ]; then
         MAIN_ROOT=$(dirname "$COMMON_ABS")
         if [ -d "$MAIN_ROOT" ] && [ "${UNDERSTAND_NO_WORKTREE_REDIRECT:-0}" != "1" ]; then
           echo "[understand] Detected git worktree at $PROJECT_ROOT"
           echo "[understand] Redirecting output to main repo root: $MAIN_ROOT"
           echo "[understand] (Set UNDERSTAND_NO_WORKTREE_REDIRECT=1 to keep PROJECT_ROOT as the worktree.)"
           PROJECT_ROOT="$MAIN_ROOT"
         fi
       fi
     fi
     ```

This script reads all `batch-*.json` files (including `batch-<i>-part-<k>.json` produced by file-analyzers that split their output) from `$UA_DIR/intermediate/`, then in one pass:

- Normalizes node IDs (strips double prefixes, project-name prefixes, adds missing prefixes)
- Normalizes complexity values (`low`→`simple`, `medium`→`moderate`, `high`→`complex`, etc.)
- Rewrites edge references to match corrected node IDs
- Deduplicates nodes by ID (keeps last occurrence) and edges by `(source, target, type)`
- Drops dangling edges referencing missing nodes
- Logs all corrections and dropped items to stderr

The merge script also runs a `tested_by` linker that canonicalizes test-coverage edges in two passes. **Pass 1** walks LLM-emitted `tested_by` edges and flips inverted ones in place; semantically broken edges (test↔test, prod↔prod, orphan endpoints) are dropped. **Pass 2** supplements with path-convention pairings. Production nodes that end up sourcing any `tested_by` edge get a `"tested"` tag. All resulting edges run `production → test`.

#### Default path (no `--review`): inline deterministic validation

Write the following Node.js script to `$UA_DIR/tmp/ua-inline-validate.cjs`:

```javascript
#!/usr/bin/env node
const fs = require('fs');
const graphPath = process.argv[2];
const outputPath = process.argv[3];
try {
  const graph = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(graphPath, 'utf8'));
  const issues = [], warnings = [];
  if (!Array.isArray(graph.nodes)) { issues.push('graph.nodes is missing or not an array'); graph.nodes = []; }
  if (!Array.isArray(graph.edges)) { issues.push('graph.edges is missing or not an array'); graph.edges = []; }
  const nodeIds = new Set();
  const seen = new Map();
  graph.nodes.forEach((n, i) => {
    if (!n.id) { issues.push(`Node[${i}] missing id`); return; }
    if (!n.type) issues.push(`Node[${i}] '${n.id}' missing type`);
    if (!n.name) issues.push(`Node[${i}] '${n.id}' missing name`);
    if (!n.summary) issues.push(`Node[${i}] '${n.id}' missing summary`);
    if (!n.tags || !n.tags.length) issues.push(`Node[${i}] '${n.id}' missing tags`);
    if (seen.has(n.id)) issues.push(`Duplicate node ID '${n.id}' at indices ${seen.get(n.id)} and ${i}`);
    else seen.set(n.id, i);
    nodeIds.add(n.id);
  });
  graph.edges.forEach((e, i) => {
    if (!nodeIds.has(e.source)) issues.push(`Edge[${i}] source '${e.source}' not found`);
    if (!nodeIds.has(e.target)) issues.push(`Edge[${i}] target '${e.target}' not found`);
  });
  const fileLevelTypes = new Set(['file', 'config', 'document', 'service', 'pipeline', 'table', 'schema', 'resource', 'endpoint']);
  const fileNodes = graph.nodes.filter(n => fileLevelTypes.has(n.type)).map(n => n.id);
  const assigned = new Map();
  if (!Array.isArray(graph.layers)) { if (graph.layers) warnings.push('graph.layers is not an array'); graph.layers = []; }
  if (!Array.isArray(graph.tour)) { if (graph.tour) warnings.push('graph.tour is not an array'); graph.tour = []; }
  graph.layers.forEach(layer => {
    (layer.nodeIds || []).forEach(id => {
      if (!nodeIds.has(id)) issues.push(`Layer '${layer.id}' refs missing node '${id}'`);
      if (assigned.has(id)) issues.push(`Node '${id}' appears in multiple layers`);
      assigned.set(id, layer.id);
    });
  });
  fileNodes.forEach(id => {
    if (!assigned.has(id)) issues.push(`File node '${id}' not in any layer`);
  });
  graph.tour.forEach((step, i) => {
    (step.nodeIds || []).forEach(id => {
      if (!nodeIds.has(id)) issues.push(`Tour step[${i}] refs missing node '${id}'`);
    });
  });
  const withEdges = new Set([
    ...graph.edges.map(e => e.source),
    ...graph.edges.map(e => e.target)
  ]);
  graph.nodes.forEach(n => {
    if (!withEdges.has(n.id)) warnings.push(`Node '${n.id}' has no edges (orphan)`);
  });
  const stats = {
    totalNodes: graph.nodes.length,
    totalEdges: graph.edges.length,
    totalLayers: graph.layers.length,
    tourSteps: graph.tour.length,
    nodeTypes: graph.nodes.reduce((a, n) => { a[n.type] = (a[n.type]||0)+1; return a; }, {}),
    edgeTypes: graph.edges.reduce((a, e) => { a[e.type] = (a[e.type]||0)+1; return a; }, {})
  };
  fs.writeFileSync(outputPath, JSON.stringify({ issues, warnings, stats }, null, 2));
  process.exit(0);
} catch (err) { process.stderr.write(err.message + '\n'); process.exit(1); }
```

During the ban period the fisher’s entries are locked and they cannot log any catch. 10. When the ban expires, the steward clears the ban status from the ledger. 11. All entries are visible to the community; the ledger’s communal_reserve_kg field reflects the total fines collected. 12. The steward’s rotation ensures no single fisher holds audit power and the process remains transparent.

**Policy**: No fisher may net more than **20 kg** per trip. Any excess must be returned on the spot, a **1 kg** fine is added to the communal reserve, and the fisher receives a **one‑week ban**. All actions are logged in the shared ledger and overseen by a rotating steward.

**Operationalization**
1. A *trip* starts when a fisher leaves the dock and ends when they return to unload.
2. Upon docking, the fisher records the total catch weight (kg) in the communal ledger with their name, date, and weight.
3. If the recorded weight exceeds **20 kg**, the fisher must immediately return the excess weight to the lake.
4. The current steward (rotating monthly) verifies the return by weighing the returned fish and records the returned weight in the ledger, then signs the entry.
5. The ledger adds **1 kg** to `communal_reserve_kg` and increments the fisher’s fine column by **1 kg**.
6. The ledger entry shows the fine, returned weight, and steward’s signature.
7. The steward reviews the ledger daily; any fisher who logs > 20 kg without returning excess is flagged for a **one‑week ban**.
8. The ban entry records fisher name, start date (current date), and end date (start + 7 days) and is displayed in the ledger.
9. During the ban period the fisher’s entries are locked; they cannot log any catch.
10. When the ban expires, the steward clears the ban status from the ledger.
11. All entries are visible to the community; `communal_reserve_kg` reflects total fines collected.
12. The steward rotation ensures no single fisher holds audit power and the process remains transparent.

2. Policy: The lake will be managed under a quarterly 5 % TAC, with each active fisher limited to 1.5 % of lake biomass per trip, penalties for excess catch moved to a steward‑held community pool used for restocking, maintenance, and community projects, and fishing ceases if biomass falls below 100 kg.

The community steward, elected annually by simple majority of active fishers, holds the pool and tracks all entries. 9. The steward, with a small audit committee, reviews the pool monthly, audits balances, and prepares a quarterly disbursement proposal (for restocking, lake maintenance, or community projects). 10. 4. Policy: Each fisher may take no more than 8 kg per trip, a maximum of 3 trips per 6‑week season, the community limits total harvest to 40 % of the lake’s initial biomass, and penalties, reserve handling, and enforcement are governed by the shared ledger, rotating trustee, and volunteer monitors as outlined below.

6. 9. Policy: Each fisher may keep up to 12 kg per trip; any fish under 8 cm must be released immediately; any weight above 12 kg is placed into the communal reserve for community expenses; if a fisher keeps a fish under 8 cm, the weight of that fish is confiscated and the fisher pays a fine equal to 1 kg of catch per violation.

The community steward, elected annually by simple majority of active fishers, holds the pool and tracks all entries. 9. The steward, with a small audit committee, reviews the pool monthly, audits balances, and prepares a quarterly disbursement proposal (for restocking, lake maintenance, or community projects). 10. All fishers have unrestricted access to the ledger and may audit the pool at any time. 12. If B < 100 kg, fishing is suspended until a subsequent survey shows recovery to ≥ 100 kg. 13. 9. Policy: Each fisher may keep up to 12 kg per trip; any fish under 8 cm must be released immediately; any weight above 12 kg is placed into the communal reserve for community expenses; if a fisher keeps a fish under 8 cm, the weight of that fish is confiscated and the fisher pays a fine equal to 1 kg of catch per violation.

If a fisher exceeds their quota, the surplus is deducted from their next trip’s quota and a reminder is issued by the next scheduled surveyor. 5. A persistent violation is defined as exceeding the 8% quota on two or more consecutive trips or accumulating an excess over a four‑week period that totals more than 4% of the lake’s current biomass. 6. Upon detection of a persistent violation, the fisher who observes it (or any fisher who reports it) calls a community meeting; the council convenes, reviews the ledger, and decides corrective actions such as temporary quota reductions or education sessions. 7. All procedures, ledger entries, and meeting minutes are publicly posted for transparency and accountability.

2. Policy: The lake will be managed under a quarterly 5 % TAC, with each active fisher limited to 1.5 % of lake biomass per trip, penalties for excess catch moved to a steward‑held community pool used for restocking, maintenance, and community projects, and fishing ceases if biomass falls below 100 kg.
   In practice: 1. Every quarter, the community conducts a lake survey to measure total biomass (B). 2. TAC = 0.05 × B. 3. The TAC is divided equally among all currently active fishing members to give each a personal quarterly quota (Qp) = TAC / (number of active fishers). 4. Each trip, a fisher may catch no more than 0.015 × B (1.5 % of current lake biomass). 5. Before leaving, the fisher records intended catch in the communal ledger; after the trip, the actual catch is logged. 6. If actual > intended, the surplus (S) is handled as follows:\n   a. If S ≤ 0.5 kg or the fisher has exceeded quota fewer than twice in the past 12 months, the surplus is deducted from that fisher’s next allocation (future quota).  b. Otherwise, the surplus is treated as a penalty and transferred to the community pool.\n7. Penalties are added to the community pool ledger. 8. The community steward, elected annually by simple majority of active fishers, holds the pool and tracks all entries. 9. The steward, with a small audit committee, reviews the pool monthly, audits balances, and prepares a quarterly disbursement proposal (for restocking, lake maintenance, or community projects). 10. The proposal is presented to the community; a simple majority vote authorises any disbursement, which is then recorded in the ledger. 11. All fishers have unrestricted access to the ledger and may audit the pool at any time. 12. If B < 100 kg, fishing is suspended until a subsequent survey shows recovery to ≥ 100 kg. 13. The steward is re‑elected each year at the first community meeting, with recall possible by simple majority if duties are not fulfilled.

3. Policy: Each fisher may harvest up to 10 kg per trip; any surplus must be returned to the lake before the boat returns to the dock. All trips are recorded in the communal ledger and the council reviews entries daily, revoking permits for those exceeding the limit more than twice per month and conducting random checks to enforce compliance.
   In practice: A trip is a continuous outing from departure to return to the dock, regardless of duration. Each fisher records departure and return timestamps, total catch weight, and any surplus deposited in the lake deposit area on the communal ledger kept at the council office. The council reviews the ledger every morning; if a fisher exceeds 10 kg more than twice in a month, their permit is revoked for the next month. Banned fishers are reinstated automatically after one month, but may appeal earlier by submitting written evidence to the council for a majority vote. Random checks may be performed at any time, with the council inspecting the ledger and verifying the deposit. All fishers have equal access to the ledger and the deposit area; disputes are resolved by council vote.

4. Policy: Each fisher may take no more than 8 kg per trip, a maximum of 3 trips per 6‑week season, the community limits total harvest to 40 % of the lake’s initial biomass, and penalties, reserve handling, and enforcement are governed by the shared ledger, rotating trustee, and volunteer monitors as outlined below.
   In practice: 1. Each fisher may take no more than 8 kg per trip. 2. The community will limit the total annual harvest to 40 % of the lake’s biomass at the start of the season. 3. The season lasts 6 weeks; each fisher may make up to 3 trips (max 24 kg). 4. After each trip the fisher submits the catch weight; the volunteer monitoring group verifies it, logs the entry on the shared ledger, and if the catch >8 kg the surplus is immediately returned to the reserve and a penalty trip is assigned. 5. At season’s end the total harvest is compared to 40 % of the lake’s initial biomass; any excess is added to the communal reserve. 6. No fishing is allowed until the reserve level in the ledger meets or exceeds the new lake’s biomass. 7. The penalty trip requires the fisher to go out to the lake, may catch up to 2 kg, and must perform a community stewardship activity (e.g., shoreline cleanup or equipment maintenance). 8. The catch from the penalty trip (if any) is deposited into the communal cellar within 24 hours, verified by the monitoring group, and logged as “Penalty Trip – [Fisher Name]” and counted against the fisher’s total trips for the season. 9. The rotating community trustee holds fish in storage, releases fish only when the reserve level in the ledger meets or exceeds the new lake’s biomass, and enforces penalties by refusing release of fish or issuing a collective halt notice if a penalty trip has not been completed or logged. 10. The volunteer monitoring group logs every trip on the shared ledger; if the reserve is below the required level, they issue a collective halt notice and no fishing is allowed until the reserve is replenished. 11. The trustee reviews the ledger weekly; if any fisher has an outstanding penalty trip, they issue a collective halt notice until the penalty trip is completed and logged.

5. Policy: Each fisher must maintain a personal reserve of at least 10 kg, may take no more than 20 kg per trip, and must record catch weight and remaining reserve immediately after each trip; failure to keep the reserve or to log the trip results in a 2 kg penalty transferred to the community pot, and any trip that yields less than 2 kg has the entire catch forfeited to the pot.
   In practice: The system stores each fisher’s reserve in the database field personalReserve. After a trip the system adds the catch weight, subtracts the 1 kg required for sustenance, and then checks that the new reserve is ≥10 kg. If the catch would bring the reserve below 10 kg, the system caps the catch to the amount that keeps the reserve at 10 kg and records the capped catch. The fisher must log the trip’s catch weight and resulting reserve in the communal ledger before the end of the day. Weekly audits compare the ledger against the database; any missing or inconsistent entry triggers a penalty: 2 kg of the fisher’s next catch is automatically deducted and added to the Community Pot ledger line. If the fisher’s next catch is <2 kg, the entire catch is moved to the Community Pot. The Community Pot is a shared crate held by the council and tracked as a separate ledger item. All adjustments and penalties are applied automatically by the system, and the fisher is notified of any penalty or required ledger correction before the next audit.

6. Policy: Limit each fisher to a maximum of 12 kg per trip and require a 20 kg reserve in the lake; each fisher records intended catch on a shared log before the trip, and if the sum of intended catches exceeds lake stock minus the reserve, the surplus S is removed one‑kilogram at a time from the largest intended catchers until S = 0; any post‑reduction haul over 12 kg must return the excess to the reserve and the fisher receives a 1 kg penalty applied to their next round’s allowed catch.
   In practice: 1. Before each round, every active fisher writes their intended catch on the community ledger (12 kg cap). 2. The fishing committee—comprised of all active fishers, a chair elected by majority vote, and a neutral elder observer—sums all intended catches. 3. If the total exceeds lake stock minus the 20 kg reserve, the committee calculates surplus S and reduces it one kilogram at a time from the largest intended catchers in descending order until S = 0. 4. Any fisher whose new intended haul exceeds 12 kg must immediately return the excess to the lake reserve. 5. After each trip, the fisher’s actual haul is weighed; the weight is compared to the logged intended catch. If the weight exceeds the intended catch, the excess fish is returned to the reserve and a 1 kg penalty is recorded for that fisher’s next round. If the weight is lower, the fisher keeps the actual haul but remains capped at 12 kg in the log. 6. The committee records all catches, reductions, penalties, and reserve contributions on a public ledger displayed for all community members. 7. In the next round, a fisher with a 1 kg penalty has their allowed catch automatically reduced from 12 kg to 11 kg (or further if multiple penalties apply). 8. Disputes are resolved by majority vote of the committee; any unresolved conflict may be escalated to the neutral elder for final arbitration.

7. Policy: Each fisher may keep up to 5 kg per trip and must release at least 1 kg; if the lake’s monthly stock falls below 50 kg the keep limit drops to 4 kg and the release requirement rises to 2 kg until the stock recovers to 50 kg or more.
   In practice: 1. Each fisher logs three numbers per trip: raw_catch_kg, kept_kg, released_kg. 2. The community ledger maintains a sub‑ledger per fisher with fields kept_kg and released_kg, and enforces rules automatically: if kept_kg>5 kg the excess is credited back to the pool and the fisher receives a one‑trip ban; if released_kg<1 kg the entire catch is confiscated and the fisher receives a one‑trip ban. 3. Miro, as the designated keeper, logs the lake’s monthly stock once a month. 4. The ledger automatically adjusts caps when the logged stock crosses the 50 kg threshold: below 50 kg, keep limit =4 kg and release requirement =2 kg; at 50 kg or above, caps revert to 5 kg keep and 1 kg release. 5. All changes and penalties are recorded in the ledger; no manual intervention is required after initial logging.

8. Policy: Each fisher may take only the lesser of 8 % of the lake’s current weight or 15 kg per trip, must deposit 1 kg into the safety bin, and may withdraw from the bin only when his personal reserve falls below 10 kg; any catch exceeding the quota results in half forfeiture and the remainder joining the communal reserve.
   In practice: 1. At the monthly committee meeting, the fishery committee records the current lake_weight in the logbook. 2. Each fisher computes his quota as min(0.08 × lake_weight, 15 kg). 3. During each trip the fisher harvests up to his quota, retains the catch in his personal_reserve, and immediately sets aside 1 kg to deposit into safety_bin_kg (personal_reserve – 1 kg). 4. If the fisher’s catch exceeds the quota, the excess is split: half is discarded (returned to the lake_weight), the other half is added to communal_reserve_kg. 5. After each outing the appointed deposit recorder logs the 1 kg deposit for each fisher, updates personal_reserve[fisher], safety_bin_kg, communal_reserve_kg, and lake_weight (subtracting kept_fish + 1 kg deposit + communal reserve additions, adding back discarded half). 6. If a fisher’s personal_reserve falls below 10 kg, the recorder, with committee approval, withdraws the necessary amount from safety_bin_kg to bring the reserve up to 10 kg, recording the withdrawal. 7. The committee reviews lake_weight monthly; if total catches stay below 10 % of lake_weight for three consecutive months, quotas are reduced in the next cycle. 8. All updates are entered into the shared logbook after each trip, ensuring transparency and traceability.

9. Policy: Each fisher may keep up to 12 kg per trip; any fish under 8 cm must be released immediately; any weight above 12 kg is placed into the communal reserve for community expenses; if a fisher keeps a fish under 8 cm, the weight of that fish is confiscated and the fisher pays a fine equal to 1 kg of catch per violation.
   In practice: Before setting off, every fisher measures each fish with a measuring tape or ruler on board; the designated ledger keeper for the day records all catches in a shared log on the boat, noting weight, length, and whether the fish is kept or released. At the end of the trip, the Lake Guardians—five rotating fishers plus the elder chair—review the log, confiscate any undersized fish kept, add the weight of any excess above 12 kg to the communal reserve chest at the dock, and record a debit for the fisher’s contribution and a credit for the communal pot in the shared ledger. The communal reserve chest is kept in a shared dock chest, its balance tracked in the ledger; when community needs gear or repairs, a disbursement entry debits the pot and credits the expense account after a majority vote of the Guardians and fishers. The ledger keeper role rotates weekly or by simple draw at the start of each trip to ensure fairness. Any fisher who fails to release a fish under 8 cm must surrender the weight of the fish back into the communal pot and pay the fine, which is enforced by the Guardians taking the weight and recording the fine in the ledger.

1: Policy: No individual fisher may catch more than 8% of the lake’s current biomass in any single trip.
2: 
3: Operationalization: 1. Every week, a fisher is rotated to the role of "biomass surveyor" by community council vote; that fisher sets up a standard 2‑m gill net, nets for 30 minutes, weighs all fish, and multiplies the haul weight by three to estimate the lake’s total biomass. 2. 3: **Policy**: No individual fisher may catch more than **8 %** of the lake’s current biomass in any single trip.
4: 
5: **Operationalization**
6: 1. Each week the community council votes a fisher to be the *biomass surveyor*.
7: 2. The surveyor sets a standard 2‑m gill net, fishes for 30 minutes, weighs the haul and multiplies by three to estimate the lake’s total biomass.
8: 3. The estimated biomass is recorded in the communal ledger with the date and surveyor’s name; this value becomes the basis for all quotas for the following week.
9: 4. Each fisher’s quota for the week is **8 %** of the recorded biomass. After each trip the fisher logs the haul weight in the ledger.
10: 5. If a fisher’s logged haul exceeds their quota, the excess is deducted from their quota for the next trip and a reminder is issued by the next scheduled surveyor.
11: 6. A *persistent violation* is defined as either:
12:    - Exceeding the quota on two or more consecutive trips, **or**
13:    - Accumulating excess weight over a four‑week period that totals more than **4 %** of the lake’s current biomass.
14: 7. Upon detection of a persistent violation, any fisher who observes it (or any fisher who reports it) calls a community meeting; the council convenes, reviews the ledger, and decides corrective actions such as temporary quota reductions or education sessions.
15: 8. All procedures, ledger entries, and meeting minutes are publicly posted for transparency and accountability.

Each fisher’s quota is 8% of that weekly estimate; they record their haul weight in the ledger after each trip. 4. If a fisher exceeds their quota, the surplus is deducted from their next trip’s quota and a reminder is issued by the next scheduled surveyor. 5. A persistent violation is defined as exceeding the 8% quota on two or more consecutive trips or accumulating an excess over a four‑week period that totals more than 4% of the lake’s current biomass. 6. Upon detection of a persistent violation, the fisher who observes it (or any fisher who reports it) calls a community meeting; the council convenes, reviews the ledger, and decides corrective actions such as temporary quota reductions or education sessions. 7. All procedures, ledger entries, and meeting minutes are publicly posted for transparency and accountability.
